verdicts.summary: Lean has a stronger form of it. `navierStokesResidual ν u p t x = temporalDerivative u t x + advection u t x - ν • spatialLaplacian u t x + pressureGradient p t x` is the paper's left-hand operator with advection = (u·∇)u, so rescale_residual at a = √ν, μ = 1 is exactly the first equality of the display: rescale (√ν) (√ν)⁻¹ u = u_ν, rescale ν (√ν)⁻¹ p = p_ν (since a^2 = ν), a^2μ = ν, and the right side is √ν • (viscosity-one residual of u, p) at y = x/√ν. The Lean statement is more general than the display: it holds for every a ≠ 0 and every μ, the paper's line being the instance a = √ν, μ = 1; `candidate_at_viscosity` performs that specialization via Real.sq_sqrt. Likewise rescale_divergence holds for every (a, b), and at a = √ν, b = (√ν)⁻¹ the prefactor a*b is 1, giving the display's ∇_x·u_ν(x,t) = (∇_y·u)(y,t); that prefactor is not simplified to 1 inside rescale_divergence itself. The two trailing equalities of the display (`= f_ν(x,t)` and `= 0`) are not in rescale_residual / rescale_divergence; they are discharged as the two proof steps of rescale_candidate cited above, from the hypothesis that u, p, f satisfy the viscosity-one equation and are divergence free. So the display is split across one general identity plus one specializing step in each of the two lines.
